name: Composite bonding

image.caption: Bonding a chipped incisor step by step - composite layers

lead: In composite bonding, a dentist shapes tooth-coloured resin onto a tooth and hardens it with a blue light. It closes small gaps, repairs chips and cracks, and masks stains, giving a more even, brighter-looking smile that shows straight away.

The resin is bonded to enamel and dentin with an adhesive, then cured. Adhesive dentistry goes back to Michael Buonocore's 1955 acid-etching work, and Irwin Smigel helped popularise using it for closing gaps and recontouring in place of crowns.

paras: It is usually done in a single visit with little or no drilling. Adhesives have moved from total-etch to self-etch and universal systems introduced in 2012, said to bond to several surfaces. Results are often polished and checked at later visits.

Wikipedia says the best longevity came from fourth-generation multi-step agents, while simpler self-etch systems were more convenient. Registered trials compare bonding agents mainly for post-operative sensitivity and restoration performance, and durability varies by material and technique.

angle.text: A dentist bonds tooth-coloured resin onto teeth to close small gaps, repair chips and cover stains, giving a more even smile in a single visit. Durability varies by material and technique.

lead: Composite bonding, also called dental bonding, is the attachment of a tooth-coloured resin to natural enamel and dentin: the dentist applies the resin, shapes it, and cures it with visible blue light so it bonds to the tooth and improves its appearance.[1] People use it to change how their smile looks without removing much tooth: it can close gaps, repair chips and cracks, lengthen or reshape short or uneven teeth, and mask discolouration, producing a more even, symmetrical smile in a single visit.[1][2]

Bonding is part of adhesive dentistry, which is used in operative, preventive, cosmetic, paediatric and prosthodontic dentistry and in orthodontics, where it attaches brackets.[1] Wikipedia dates adhesive dentistry to Michael Buonocore's 1955 acid-etching paper, and credits Irwin Smigel with broadening cosmetic use to close gaps between teeth, lengthen teeth and recontour the whole mouth in place of crowns.[1]

Published research is mostly about adhesives and restorative composites in general, such as lab bond-strength testing and trials in cavities, rather than the cosmetic reshaping of front teeth specifically.[3][4][5] A few papers address the cosmetic setting directly, including a systematic review of how polishing affects the surface roughness, and so the staining risk, of direct anterior composite restorations.[6]

Composite bonding sits at the conservative, lower-commitment end of cosmetic dentistry. Wikipedia's veneer article lists it alongside crowns, cosmetic contouring and orthodontics as an alternative to porcelain veneers, which usually involve shaving some enamel and are made in a laboratory, whereas bonding is built directly on the tooth and, as the cosmetic dentistry article notes, can be reshaped and bonded in one office visit.[7][8] Recent case reports describe the same direct approach used to close multiple gaps across ten front teeth and to finish smile-line changes after gum contouring.[9][10]

paras: Direct composite bonding uses tooth-coloured composite placed directly onto the tooth in the mouth, as opposed to indirect restorations made in a laboratory. Wikipedia lists direct composites as used to fill cavities, close diastemas (gaps), reshape teeth and make partial crowns.[2] Cosmetic bonding is the additive version of this: the dentist builds up resin on the visible surface of a tooth to change its form.[1][2]

A 1997 review of restorative options for young patients with missing front teeth lists recontouring, bleaching and resin composite bonding among the modern modalities that can improve the result after orthodontic space closure, with veneers and crowns indicated in harder situations.[11] A 2020 review describes transitional direct composite bonding as an additive option for interim restorations when restoring bite height and function, noting that it is time consuming.[12] A patient-education handout in the Journal of Esthetic and Restorative Dentistry also covers composite bonding for patients.[13]

Wikipedia traces bonding agents from no-etch to total-etch (fourth and fifth generation) and then to self-etch systems (sixth and seventh generation), which reduced sensitivity to operator error. Universal adhesives, introduced in 2012, are said to bond to enamel, dentin, metal, porcelain, ceramic and zirconia in a single application, though the term has no settled definition [1].

A review of restorative composites reports that nanofiller particles enhance the properties of various reinforced composites, including mechanical strength and physical properties [4]. A guidance paper from the Academy of Dental Materials addresses in vitro micro-tensile bond strength testing of dental adhesives to enamel and dentin [14].

Dental composites have three main parts: a resin matrix (commonly Bis-GMA with other dimethacrylates), glass or silica filler particles that add strength, wear resistance and translucency, and a silane coupling agent that links filler to resin, with a photoinitiator such as camphorquinone that starts setting under blue light.[2] Filler types are described as macrofilled, microfilled, hybrid, nanofilled or bulk-fill, and a review reports that nanofiller particles improve the mechanical properties of dental composites and that silane-treated filler improved bonding strength.[4][2]

The material bonds micromechanically to enamel and dentin, which Wikipedia says means less healthy tooth has to be removed, and it can be matched to the tooth over a wide shade range, which matters most in front teeth.[2] Curing light penetrates about 2 to 3 mm, so thicker build-ups are placed and cured in increments, and the tooth must be kept dry during placement.[2]

Dental composites appeared in the late 1960s as an alternative to silicates and unfilled resins; early versions had poor appearance and were difficult to polish. Light-curing arrived in the 1970s, microfilled composites in 1978 and hybrids in the 1980s, with bonding to dentin improving in the 1990s and 2000s.[2] Adhesive dentistry itself began with Buonocore's 1955 paper on acid etching, followed by bonding agents that moved from no-etch to total-etch and then self-etch systems.[1] Irwin Smigel, a founder of the American Society for Dental Aesthetics, was among the first to use bonding to close gaps and recontour teeth rather than use crowns, and in 1979 published a guide titled Dental Health/Dental Beauty.[1]

Veneers are thin custom laminates of porcelain or composite that cover the front surface of a tooth. Wikipedia reports that porcelain veneers are more durable and less likely to stain than composite ones, that composite veneers have a lifespan of about four years, and that with modern cements porcelain veneers typically last 10 to 30 years, although the same article cites a finding that about half of veneers are displaced, need re-treatment or are unsatisfactory after 10 years.[7] Those figures describe veneers rather than every form of bonding, and published durability varies with the material, the tooth and the patient's bite habits.[2][7]

The appeal of bonding in these comparisons is that it is additive. The veneer article says preparing a tooth for a porcelain veneer often means shaving enamel, which can cause sensitivity and decay, and that an inexperienced dentist may remove 3 to 30 percent of the tooth surface; the cosmetic dentistry article likewise notes that enamel removed during reshaping cannot be replaced.[7][8] Composite bonds micromechanically and needs little removal of healthy tooth, and the same sources describe composite veneers as a common choice for adolescents who will later need a more permanent solution.[2][7] Critics quoted in the veneer article say some practitioners overuse veneers for what they call instant orthodontics in people with healthy teeth, and list alternatives such as composite bonding and contouring.[7]

sections.h: Direct composite veneers in recent case reports
paras: Case reports from 2026 illustrate how bonding is used for smile design. One describes a 22-year-old with diastemas treated with ten direct composite veneers from tooth 15 to tooth 25 using a dual-matrix technique; all restorations scored Alpha on the FDI criteria at baseline, and at 12 months mild interproximal staining, marginal discolouration and loss of surface luster were noted, plus one incisal chip corrected at the chair, with no secondary decay.[9] Another case series of two patients combined crown lengthening for excessive gum display with direct nanocomposite veneers; pink and white esthetic scores improved, and at about 24 months there was minor chipping and mild plaque-related gum inflammation, with the authors noting that long-term colour stability data are lacking.[10] These are individual cases rather than controlled trials.

The American Dental Association does not recognise cosmetic dentistry as a formal specialty, according to Wikipedia, and the article says prosthodontics is the specialty under which aesthetic work falls; it also reports that many dentists describe themselves as cosmetic dentists regardless of training, which it describes as an ethical concern, and that some question whether general dentists should handle complex smile makeovers.[8] The article credits Newell Sill Jenkins (1840-1919), an American dentist working in Dresden, with developing a porcelain enamel and regards him as the founder of aesthetic dentistry.[8]

The Wikipedia article says the best bonding and longevity came from fourth-generation agents, which use separate etch, prime and bond steps, but gives no other durability figures [1]. It also cites a Cochrane review finding no clear evidence for choosing one orthodontic adhesive over another [1].

Wikipedia reports annual failure rates of roughly 1 to 3 percent for posterior composites in Class I and II restorations in one 2012 review, cites main failure causes as secondary decay, fracture and bruxism, and notes that failure definitions strongly affect figures; these figures are for posterior fillings rather than cosmetic front-tooth work.[2] Composites can chip or wear under heavy forces and are repairable by adding material.[2] Polymerisation shrinkage can lead to microleakage, and results depend on operator skill and moisture control.[2]

The 2023 systematic review of direct anterior composites notes that these restorations are an esthetic, minimally invasive option but that longevity remains a challenge because staining can be influenced by the surface roughness left after polishing, which can depend on the combination of composite and polishing system.[6] Studies of bleaching report that the shear bond strength of composite to freshly bleached enamel can be affected, and an in vitro study tested three antioxidants for restoring it.[3]

No studies found of composite bonding specifically for masking stains and chips for cosmetic purposes. Registered trials involve related adhesive questions, such as comparing fifth- and eighth-generation bonding agents for post-operative sensitivity in class I restorations [5], clinical evaluation of a two-step universal adhesive in non-carious cervical lesions [15], and comparison of adhesive systems containing HEMA and 10-MDP in such lesions [16]. A further registered trial examines tooth discoloration and handling time of flowable versus packable composites for clear aligner attachments [17].

Older clinical work includes a 1992 three-year evaluation of a light-cured composite and bonding system in 60 Class I and II restorations,[18] and a 2024 split-mouth randomised trial compared bond failure of orthodontic brackets with two adhesive systems;[19] these concern function and bond failure rather than appearance.

Laboratory work continues on pretreatments and adhesives: a 2025 meta-analysis of 13 in vitro studies found Er:YAG laser pretreatment of dentin gave bond strength comparable with mechanical preparation but lower than conventional etch-and-rinse, and higher than untreated dentin.[20] Registered trials are comparing bulk-fill and conventional composites for orthodontic brackets and nanoparticle-containing bonding agents for post-restorative sensitivity.[21][22]

timeline.event: Dentist Charles Pincus makes veneers to alter actors' teeth for a film shoot, an early step toward cosmetic bonding of the front teeth.[7]
Michael Buonocore publishes the acid-etching paper that began adhesive dentistry.[1]
Dental composites appear as an alternative to silicates and unfilled resins.[2]
Light-curing replaces two-paste chemical curing; microfilled composites follow in 1978.[2]
Irwin Smigel publishes a guide to aesthetic dentistry.[1]
